terms.def: An absolute (global) maximum is a value <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(c)</annotation></semantics></math> with <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≥</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(c) \ge f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> for every <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> in the domain or interval considered; an absolute minimum has <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≤</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(c) \le f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> for every such <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Extreme Value Theorem, Global and Local Extrema, Critical Points

terms.def: The rate of change of velocity: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">″</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a(t) = v'(t) = x''(t)</annotation></semantics></math>. Units: distance per time per time, such as meters per second per second.

The total change in an amount over an interval of time, built up from its rate of change. On a graph of the rate, it is the area between the graph and the horizontal axis: area above the axis adds, area below subtracts. Its units are the rate's units times the input's units.

A function defined by a definite integral with a variable limit, such as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g(x)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></msubsup><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \int_a^x f(t)\,dt</annotation></semantics></math>: the amount accumulated from <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> up to <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>. It is 0 at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = a</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: The Fundamental Theorem and Accumulation Functions

terms.def: A function <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math> whose derivative is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F'(x) = f(x)</annotation></semantics></math>. For example, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^2 + 5</annotation></semantics></math> is an antiderivative of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2x</annotation></semantics></math>. Any two antiderivatives of the same function on an interval differ by a constant.
terms.topicTitle: The Fundamental Theorem and Accumulation Functions

terms.def: Choosing how to find an antiderivative: try a basic rule (after rewriting powers or splitting over a single term), then substitution (an inside function whose derivative is a factor), then long division (top degree at least bottom degree), then completing the square (a quadratic with no real zeros on the bottom). Check by differentiating.

The area of the region bounded by two graphs: on an interval where <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≥</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x) \ge g(x)</annotation></semantics></math>, it is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int_a^b \left(f(x) - g(x)\right)\,dx</annotation></semantics></math>, top minus bottom, with limits where the region starts and ends (often where the curves meet).

A line the graph approaches. A rational function has a vertical asymptote <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = a</annotation></semantics></math> where its denominator is 0 and its numerator is not; a horizontal asymptote is a height the outputs settle toward as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|x|</annotation></semantics></math> grows large.

The change in a quantity divided by the change in the input over an interval: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}</annotation></semantics></math>. It is the slope of the line through <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a, f(a))</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(b, f(b))</annotation></semantics></math>, in output units per input unit.
terms.topicTitle: Can Change Happen at an Instant?

terms.def: The average value of a function <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> on <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[a, b]</annotation></semantics></math> is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{b - a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx</annotation></semantics></math>: the height of the rectangle on <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[a, b]</annotation></semantics></math> with the same signed area as the region under <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>. It has the units of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>.

A way to find the absolute extrema of a function continuous on <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[a, b]</annotation></semantics></math>: evaluate <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> at the endpoints <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> and at every critical point in <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a, b)</annotation></semantics></math>; the largest value is the absolute maximum and the smallest the absolute minimum. Also called the closed interval method.

The rule for differentiating a composite function: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d}{dx} f(g(x))</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>⋅</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= f'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x)</annotation></semantics></math>. The derivative of the outside function <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>, evaluated at the inside function <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g(x)</annotation></semantics></math>, times the derivative of the inside function.

A fraction whose top or bottom contains fractions, such as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mi>x</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\frac{1}{x + 2} - \frac{1}{2}}{x}</annotation></semantics></math>. Combine the inner fractions over a common denominator to simplify it.
terms.topicTitle: Algebra for Limits: Factoring and Rationalizing

terms.def: A composite function feeds one output into another function: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(g(x))</annotation></semantics></math> applies <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> first, then <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>.

A graph is concave up on an interval where <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">″</mo></mrow><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'' > 0</annotation></semantics></math> (it bends upward and lies above its tangent lines) and concave down where <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">″</mo></mrow><mo><</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'' < 0</annotation></semantics></math> (it bends downward and lies below them).

The basic derivative rules: the constant rule <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d}{dx}(c) = 0</annotation></semantics></math>; the constant multiple rule <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d}{dx}\left( kf(x) \right) = kf'(x)</annotation></semantics></math>; and the sum and difference rules <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>±</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d}{dx}\left( f(x) \pm g(x) \right)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>±</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= f'(x) \pm g'(x)</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Constant, Sum, Difference and Constant Multiple Rules

terms.def: In an optimization problem, a fixed condition that links the variables, such as a given perimeter, volume or budget. It is used to write the objective function in terms of one variable.

A function is continuous on an open interval when it is continuous at every point of it. On a closed interval <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[a, b]</annotation></semantics></math> it must also be continuous from the inside at each endpoint: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow></munder><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= f(a)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></mrow></munder><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{x \to b^-} f(x)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= f(b)</annotation></semantics></math>.

A point where a continuous graph has no derivative: a corner (the left and right slopes are different numbers, as for <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|x|</annotation></semantics></math> at 0), a cusp (the slopes grow without bound in opposite directions, as for <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{2/3}</annotation></semantics></math> at 0) or a vertical tangent line (as for <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mroot><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></mroot></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt[3]{x}</annotation></semantics></math> at 0).

An interior point <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> of the domain of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> where <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'(c) = 0</annotation></semantics></math> or <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'(c)</annotation></semantics></math> does not exist. Relative extrema can occur only at critical points.
terms.topicTitle: Extreme Value Theorem, Global and Local Extrema, Critical Points

terms.def: The flat shape you get by slicing a solid with a plane, here perpendicular to an axis. If the slice at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> has area <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A(x)</annotation></semantics></math>, the solid's volume is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int_a^b A(x)\,dx</annotation></semantics></math>. For squares with side <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s(x)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A(x) = s(x)^2</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Volumes with Square and Rectangle Cross Sections

terms.def: The limit of Riemann sums of a function <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> on <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[a, b]</annotation></semantics></math> as the widths of the subintervals shrink to 0, written <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int_a^b f(x)\,dx</annotation></semantics></math>. The function <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> is the integrand; <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> are the limits of integration. For a positive <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> it is the area under the graph; for a rate, the accumulated change.
terms.topicTitle: Riemann Sums, Sigma Notation and the Definite Integral

terms.def: A function <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is continuous at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = c</annotation></semantics></math> when three conditions hold: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(c)</annotation></semantics></math> is defined, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></munder><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{x \to c} f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> exists, and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></munder><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{x \to c} f(x)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= f(c)</annotation></semantics></math>.

The instantaneous rate of change of a function. At <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = a</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'(a)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></munder><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>h</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}</annotation></semantics></math> when the limit exists; found at every <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, it is the derivative function <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'(x)</annotation></semantics></math>.

The meaning of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'(a)</annotation></semantics></math> in a real situation: the rate at which the quantity <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> changes at input <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math>, in units of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> per unit of the input (for example, centimeters per hour).

The derivative of the inverse of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left(f^{-1}\right)'(a)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{1}{f'\left(f^{-1}(a)\right)}</annotation></semantics></math>, provided <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'\left(f^{-1}(a)\right) \ne 0</annotation></semantics></math>. The slope of the inverse at a point is the reciprocal of the slope of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> at the reflected point.

The derivatives of the inverse trigonometric functions: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mi>arcsin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d}{dx}\arcsin x</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mi>arccos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d}{dx}\arccos x</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= -\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}</annotation></semantics></math> for <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo><</mo><mi>x</mi><mo><</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1 < x < 1</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mi>arctan</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d}{dx}\arctan x</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{1}{1 + x^2}</annotation></semantics></math>.

The four basic derivatives: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d}{dx}(\sin x) = \cos x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d}{dx}(\cos x) = -\sin x</annotation></semantics></math> (in radians), <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d}{dx}\left( e^x \right) = e^x</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>x</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d}{dx}(\ln x) = \frac{1}{x}</annotation></semantics></math> for <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x > 0</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Derivatives of sin x, cos x, e to the x and ln x

stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>tan</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>sec</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0" encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d}{dx}(\cot x) = -\csc^2 x</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>sec</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d}{dx}(\sec x)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>sec</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>tan</mi><mo lspace="0" form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>csc</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>cot</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation terms.topicTitle: Derivatives of tan, cot, sec and csc

terms.def: The average rate of change of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> between <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = a</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = a + h</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>h</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}</annotation></semantics></math> for <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h \ne 0</annotation></semantics></math>. Its limit as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h \to 0</annotation></semantics></math> is the instantaneous rate of change at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Average and Instantaneous Rates of Change

terms.def: A function is differentiable at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = a</annotation></semantics></math> when <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'(a)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></munder><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>h</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}</annotation></semantics></math> exists as a finite number, and differentiable on an interval when it is differentiable at every point of it. Differentiable implies continuous; the converse is false.

An equation that contains the derivative of an unknown function, such as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{dy}{dt} = 0.3y</annotation></semantics></math>. It says how fast a quantity changes, often in terms of the quantity itself.

Choosing which differentiation rule to apply first by finding the last operation in the expression (sum, product, quotient or composition), then repeating the choice on each piece; rewriting first when it removes a rule.

Finding <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></munder><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{x \to a} f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> by evaluating <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(a)</annotation></semantics></math>. It is justified for polynomials, and for rational, root and similar functions at points where the formula is defined (no zero denominator).

A way to find the volume of a solid of revolution whose slices are solid discs: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>π</mi><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \pi\int_a^b r(x)^2\,dx</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> is the distance from the axis of rotation to the curve. About the <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>-axis, the discs are horizontal and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>π</mi><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>c</mi><mi>d</mi></msubsup><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \pi\int_c^d r(y)^2\,dy</annotation></semantics></math>.

A point where a function is not continuous: its graph breaks there. At <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = c</annotation></semantics></math> this happens when <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(c)</annotation></semantics></math> is undefined, when <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></munder><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{x \to c} f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> does not exist, or when the two are not equal.

The change in position of a particle over a time interval: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x(b) - x(a)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \int_a^b v(t)\,dt</annotation></semantics></math>. It can be positive, negative or zero.
The set of inputs a function accepts. The range is the set of outputs it produces.

The term that grows fastest as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x \to \infty</annotation></semantics></math> and so decides a limit at infinity. In the long run <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln x</annotation></semantics></math> grows slower than any positive power of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, a higher power beats a lower one, and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^x</annotation></semantics></math> beats every power.
terms.topicTitle: Limits at Infinity and Horizontal Asymptotes

terms.def: A constant function <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = c</annotation></semantics></math> that solves a differential equation: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{dy}{dx} = 0</annotation></semantics></math> at every point of the horizontal line <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = c</annotation></semantics></math>. In a slope field it is a row of horizontal segments.

The laws for powers of one base: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>m</mi></msup><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^m x^n = x^{m+n}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>m</mi></msup><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{x^m}{x^n} = x^{m-n}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>m</mi></msup><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x^m)^n = x^{mn}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^0 = 1</annotation></semantics></math>. A negative exponent is a reciprocal (<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{-n} = \frac{1}{x^n}</annotation></semantics></math>); a fractional exponent is a root (<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mroot><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></mroot><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{m/n} = (\sqrt[n]{x})^m</annotation></semantics></math>).

A function <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mi>x</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b^x</annotation></semantics></math> with a fixed positive base <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b \ne 1</annotation></semantics></math>; it changes by the same factor over equal steps in <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>. The natural exponential <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^x</annotation></semantics></math> uses <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>≈</mo><mn>2.71828</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e \approx 2.71828</annotation></semantics></math>. <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A e^{kt}</annotation></semantics></math> shows exponential growth when <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k > 0</annotation></semantics></math> and exponential decay when <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo><</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k < 0</annotation></semantics></math>.

A quantity whose rate of change is proportional to its size, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{dy}{dt} = ky</annotation></semantics></math>, so that <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = y_0e^{kt}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_0 = y(0)</annotation></semantics></math>. The constant <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> is the growth constant (<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k > 0</annotation></semantics></math>) or decay constant (<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo><</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k < 0</annotation></semantics></math>): the rate of change as a fraction of the current amount, per unit of time.

If <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is continuous on a closed interval <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[a, b]</annotation></semantics></math>, then <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> has at least one absolute maximum value and at least one absolute minimum value on <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[a, b]</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Extreme Value Theorem, Global and Local Extrema, Critical Points

terms.def: Writing an expression as a product, such as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^2 - 9 = (x - 3)(x + 3)</annotation></semantics></math> (a difference of squares). A factored form shows which factors can cancel.
terms.topicTitle: Algebra for Limits: Factoring and Rationalizing

terms.def: At a critical point <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> where <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is continuous: if <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'</annotation></semantics></math> changes from positive to negative at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> has a relative maximum at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>; from negative to positive, a relative minimum; if <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'</annotation></semantics></math> does not change sign, no relative extremum. A sign chart of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'</annotation></semantics></math> organizes the test; the justification is a sentence naming <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'</annotation></semantics></math> and its sign change.

A rule that assigns exactly one output to each input. <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(3)</annotation></semantics></math> is the output when the input is 3.

The link between derivatives and integrals. Part 1: if <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is continuous, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></msubsup><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^x f(t)\,dt</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= f(x)</annotation></semantics></math>, and with a function as the upper limit, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^{u(x)} f(t)\,dt</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= f(u(x))\,u'(x)</annotation></semantics></math>. Part 2 (topic 6.7): <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int_a^b f(x)\,dx</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= F(b) - F(a)</annotation></semantics></math> for any antiderivative <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math> of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: The Fundamental Theorem and Accumulation Functions

terms.def: All points <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x, f(x))</annotation></semantics></math> for <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> in the domain. The height of the graph above <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = a</annotation></semantics></math> is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(a)</annotation></semantics></math>; a filled dot is on the graph, an open circle is not.

The graph of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = f'(x)</annotation></semantics></math>, whose height at each <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> is the slope of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> there. It is above the axis where <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> rises, crosses zero at the flat peaks and valleys of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>, rises where <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is concave up, and turns at the inflection points of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>.

A change that moves or reshapes a graph: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x - h) + k</annotation></semantics></math> shifts it <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> right and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> up; <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> flips it over the <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>-axis; <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> stretches it vertically.

Reading the behavior of a function from any representation of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'</annotation></semantics></math> or <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">″</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f''</annotation></semantics></math>: the sign of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'</annotation></semantics></math> gives where <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> increases or decreases, the sign of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">″</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f''</annotation></semantics></math> (or whether <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'</annotation></semantics></math> rises or falls) gives concavity, and sign changes locate relative extrema and points of inflection.

A point of a curve where the tangent line is horizontal: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{dy}{dx} = 0</annotation></semantics></math>. For an implicit curve with <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>N</mi><mi>D</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{N}{D}</annotation></semantics></math>, the numerator <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> is 0, the denominator <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> is not, and the point lies on the curve. (Where <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D = 0</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N \ne 0</annotation></semantics></math>, the tangent line is vertical instead.)

A condition a theorem needs before its conclusion can be used. For the Intermediate Value Theorem the hypotheses are that <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is continuous on the closed interval <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[a, b]</annotation></semantics></math> and that <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> is between <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(a)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(b)</annotation></semantics></math>. If a hypothesis fails, the theorem promises nothing.

Finding <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{dy}{dx}</annotation></semantics></math> from an equation in <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> without solving for <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>: differentiate both sides with respect to <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, using the chain rule on every term that holds <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>, then solve for <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{dy}{dx}</annotation></semantics></math>.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is increasing on an interval if <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo><</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x_1) < f(x_2)</annotation></semantics></math> whenever <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo><</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_1 < x_2</annotation></semantics></math> in the interval, and decreasing if <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>></mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x_1) > f(x_2)</annotation></semantics></math>. If <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'(x) > 0</annotation></semantics></math> on an interval, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is increasing there; if <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo><</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'(x) < 0</annotation></semantics></math>, it is decreasing.
terms.topicTitle: Where a Function Increases or Decreases

terms.def: The family of all antiderivatives of a function, written <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int f(x)\,dx = F(x) + C</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F' = f</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math>, the constant of integration, is any constant. It has no limits and is a family of functions, not a number.

A result like <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>0</mn><mn>0</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{0}{0}</annotation></semantics></math> from substituting into a limit. It does not determine the limit; the expression must be rewritten (factored, rationalized, simplified) first.
terms.topicTitle: Limits by Algebra: Factor, Rationalize, Simplify

terms.def: A discontinuity at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = c</annotation></semantics></math> where the function is unbounded on at least one side of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>. The graph has a vertical asymptote <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = c</annotation></semantics></math>.

A limit in which the values of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> grow without bound as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> approaches <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></munder><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = \infty</annotation></semantics></math> (or <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\infty</annotation></semantics></math>). It is a way of describing a limit that does not exist; it gives the graph a vertical asymptote <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = c</annotation></semantics></math>.
How fast a quantity is changing at one instant: the number that average rates of change over shorter and shorter intervals around that instant close in on.
terms.topicTitle: Can Change Happen at an Instant?
aka: rate of change at an instant

terms.def: Finding an area with horizontal strips: write each edge as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> in terms of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>, and integrate right minus left, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>c</mi><mi>d</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mtext>right</mtext></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mtext>left</mtext></msub></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int_c^d \left(x_{\text{right}} - x_{\text{left}}\right)\,dy</annotation></semantics></math>, between <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>-values. Best when each side edge is one formula.

The Intermediate Value Theorem: if <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is continuous on <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[a, b]</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> is a number between <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(a)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(b)</annotation></semantics></math>, then <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(c) = d</annotation></semantics></math> for at least one <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> in <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a, b)</annotation></semantics></math>.

For a one-to-one function <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>, the function <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> that undoes it: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{-1}(b) = a</annotation></semantics></math> exactly when <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(a) = b</annotation></semantics></math>. Its graph is the reflection of the graph of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> across <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = x</annotation></semantics></math>. A function is one-to-one when no two inputs share an output.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>arcsin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\arcsin x</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>arccos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\arccos x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>arctan</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\arctan x</annotation></semantics></math> (also written <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>sin</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sin^{-1} x</annotation></semantics></math>, ...) give the angle with a given sine, cosine or tangent, from a restricted range: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">[</mo><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]</annotation></semantics></math> for arcsine, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0, \pi]</annotation></semantics></math> for arccosine, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)</annotation></semantics></math> for arctangent.

A discontinuity at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = c</annotation></semantics></math> where both one-sided limits exist as finite numbers but are not equal, so the graph jumps from one height to another.

If <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim f(x) = 0</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim g(x) = 0</annotation></semantics></math>, or both limits are infinite, then <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \lim\frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}</annotation></semantics></math>, provided the limit on the right exists (or is infinite). The derivatives of the top and bottom are taken separately.

Writing the derivative of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{dy}{dx}</annotation></semantics></math>, and "the derivative of" as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d}{dx}</annotation></semantics></math>. Its value at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = a</annotation></semantics></math> is written <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">|</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=a}</annotation></semantics></math>.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></munder><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L</annotation></semantics></math> means the values <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> get as close to <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> as we like when <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> is close enough to <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> (but not equal to <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math>). The value <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(a)</annotation></semantics></math> plays no part.
terms.topicTitle: What a Limit Is and How to Write It

terms.def: Reading a limit of the form <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></munder><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>h</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}</annotation></semantics></math> or <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></munder><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}</annotation></semantics></math> as the derivative <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'(a)</annotation></semantics></math>, and evaluating it with a derivative rule.
terms.topicTitle: Derivatives of sin x, cos x, e to the x and ln x

terms.def: The value <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> approaches as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> grows without bound: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></munder><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = L</annotation></semantics></math> (or as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x \to -\infty</annotation></semantics></math>). A finite limit at infinity gives the horizontal asymptote <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = L</annotation></semantics></math>; these limits describe the end behavior of a function.
terms.topicTitle: Limits at Infinity and Horizontal Asymptotes

terms.def: A limit does not exist (DNE) when the outputs do not close in on one number: the one-sided limits differ, the outputs grow without bound, or they oscillate.

Rules that combine limits that exist: the limit of a sum, difference, constant multiple, product or power is the same combination of the limits; a quotient's limit is the quotient of the limits when the denominator's limit is not 0.

A plan for finding a limit: substitute first, then let the result decide the next step. A number is the limit; <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>0</mn><mn>0</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{0}{0}</annotation></semantics></math> means rewrite (factor, use a conjugate, combine fractions) and substitute again; a nonzero number over 0 means the function is unbounded there; a break point means compare the one-sided limits.
terms.topicTitle: Choosing a Way to Find a Limit
