terms.def: The tangent line used to approximate a function near a point: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L(x)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≈</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x) \approx L(x)</annotation></semantics></math> for <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> near <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math>. Also called local linear approximation or tangent line approximation.

Rewriting an integrand so a basic rule applies. Polynomial long division turns a fraction whose top has degree at least the bottom's into a polynomial plus a remainder fraction. Completing the square turns a quadratic with no real zeros into <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>h</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x - h)^2 + a^2</annotation></semantics></math>, which leads to an arctan form.
terms.topicTitle: Integrating by Long Division and Completing the Square

terms.def: If <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is continuous on <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[a, b]</annotation></semantics></math> and differentiable on <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a, b)</annotation></semantics></math>, then there is at least one <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> in <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a, b)</annotation></semantics></math> with <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'(c)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}</annotation></semantics></math>: the tangent line at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> is parallel to the secant line.

The ways one function can be given: a graph, a table of values, a formula, or words. A limit can be read or estimated from each one; an exam question often gives one representation and asks about another.
terms.topicTitle: Limits Across Graphs, Tables and Formulas

terms.def: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln x</annotation></semantics></math> is the power of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>e</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math> that gives <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln x = y</annotation></semantics></math> means <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>y</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^y = x</annotation></semantics></math>. It is defined for <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x > 0</annotation></semantics></math>. Log rules: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mfrac><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln\frac{a}{b} = \ln a - \ln b</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>p</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln a^p = p\ln a</annotation></semantics></math>.

The Fundamental Theorem read in context: the integral of a rate of change is the net change, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int_a^b f'(x)\,dx</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= f(b) - f(a)</annotation></semantics></math>. So <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(b)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= f(a)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">+</mo><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+ \int_a^b f'(x)\,dx</annotation></semantics></math>: the value at the end is the starting value plus the accumulated change.
terms.topicTitle: The Fundamental Theorem and Definite Integrals

terms.def: An estimate of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'(a)</annotation></semantics></math> computed from values of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> instead of a formula for <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'</annotation></semantics></math>: a difference quotient from a table, or a graphing calculator's built-in derivative, which uses <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>h</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{f(a + h) - f(a - h)}{2h}</annotation></semantics></math> with a very small <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Estimating a Derivative at a Point

terms.def: An estimate of a limit from a table of values: the number the outputs approach as the inputs get closer and closer to <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> from both sides.

The limit as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> approaches <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> from one side only: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo></msup></mrow></munder><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> uses <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo><</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x < a</annotation></semantics></math> (left-hand limit) and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow></munder><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> uses <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>></mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x > a</annotation></semantics></math> (right-hand limit).

Finding the absolute maximum or minimum value of a quantity in context. The quantity is written as an objective function of one variable on a sensible domain, and its absolute extremum is found and justified with derivatives.
Whether an approximation is too large (an overestimate) or too small (an underestimate) compared with the true value. For a tangent line approximation it follows from concavity.

The one member of a general solution that satisfies an initial condition such as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y(0) = 1</annotation></semantics></math> (a point the curve must pass through), together with its domain: the largest open interval containing the initial <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> on which the solution is defined and differentiable.

A function defined by different formulas on different parts of its domain, such as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x) = x^2</annotation></semantics></math> for <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo><</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x < 2</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x) = 3x - 1</annotation></semantics></math> for <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x \ge 2</annotation></semantics></math>.

A point on the graph of a continuous function where the concavity changes, from concave up to concave down or the reverse. For a twice-differentiable <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">″</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f''</annotation></semantics></math> changes sign there; equivalently, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'</annotation></semantics></math> changes from increasing to decreasing or back.

The point-slope form of a line with slope <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> through <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x_1, y_1)</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)</annotation></semantics></math>. Slope-intercept form is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = mx + b</annotation></semantics></math>.

A function <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x(t)</annotation></semantics></math> giving the location of an object moving along a line at time <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, measured from a fixed origin, positive in one direction and negative in the other.

For any real number <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>r</mi></msup><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d}{dx}\left( x^r \right) = r x^{r - 1}</annotation></semantics></math>: bring the exponent down and lower it by one. Roots and reciprocals are rewritten as powers first, such as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><mi>x</mi></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{x} = x^{1/2}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{x^2} = x^{-2}</annotation></semantics></math>.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d}{dx}\left( f(x)g(x) \right)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= f'(x)g(x)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">+</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+ f(x)g'(x)</annotation></semantics></math>: the derivative of the first factor times the second, plus the first times the derivative of the second. It is not <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'(x)g'(x)</annotation></semantics></math>.

Rules for definite integrals: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>a</mi></msubsup><mi>f</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int_a^a f = 0</annotation></semantics></math>; <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>a</mi></msubsup><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int_b^a f</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= -\int_a^b f</annotation></semantics></math>; additivity, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int_a^b f</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">+</mo><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>c</mi></msubsup><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+ \int_b^c f</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi></msubsup><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \int_a^c f</annotation></semantics></math>; and linearity, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int_a^b (kf + g)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>k</mi><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= k\int_a^b f</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">+</mo><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mi>g</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+ \int_a^b g</annotation></semantics></math>. Integrals split over sums and constant multiples, never over products.

"<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> is proportional to <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>" means <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A = kB</annotation></semantics></math> for a constant <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>, the constant of proportionality. "Inversely proportional to <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>" means <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>k</mi><mi>B</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A = \frac{k}{B}</annotation></semantics></math>.

An equation true for every angle. The Pythagorean identity <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>sin</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>cos</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1</annotation></semantics></math> comes from the unit circle; dividing by <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>cos</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cos^2\theta</annotation></semantics></math> gives <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>tan</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>sec</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tan^2\theta + 1 = \sec^2\theta</annotation></semantics></math>.

In a right triangle with legs <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> and hypotenuse <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^2 + b^2 = c^2</annotation></semantics></math>.

<math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d}{dx}\left( \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} \right)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msup><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{f'(x)g(x) - f(x)g'(x)}{\left( g(x) \right)^2}</annotation></semantics></math> wherever <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g(x) \ne 0</annotation></semantics></math>: derivative of the top times the bottom, minus the top times the derivative of the bottom, over the bottom squared.

A measure of angle: the length of the arc the angle cuts on a circle of radius 1. A full turn is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\pi</annotation></semantics></math> radians, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> radians <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>180</mn><mo>∘</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 180^{\circ}</annotation></semantics></math>.

The rate in (inflow rate) is how fast a quantity is added; the rate out (outflow rate) is how fast it is removed. The amount changes at rate in minus rate out, so amount at time <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> = amount at the start + <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int</annotation></semantics></math> (rate in − rate out).

The derivative of a quantity in a real setting other than motion (temperature, cost, population, volume): how fast the quantity changes per unit of input, with units, and with its sign telling whether the quantity is increasing or decreasing.
terms.topicTitle: Rates of Change in Other Contexts

terms.def: A quotient of two polynomials, such as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{2x + 1}{x - 4}</annotation></semantics></math>. A polynomial is a sum of terms <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a x^n</annotation></semantics></math> with whole-number powers <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>.

Removing a square root from part of a fraction by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><mi>A</mi></msqrt><mo>−</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{A} - B</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><mi>A</mi></msqrt><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{A} + B</annotation></semantics></math> are conjugates, and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mi>A</mi></msqrt><mo>−</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mi>A</mi></msqrt><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\sqrt{A} - B)(\sqrt{A} + B)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>B</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= A - B^2</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Algebra for Limits: Factoring and Rationalizing

terms.def: Rates of change of quantities that are linked by an equation. Differentiating the equation with respect to time <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> (chain rule on every changing variable) gives an equation linking their rates, such as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>A</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{dA}{dt} = 2\pi r\frac{dr}{dt}</annotation></semantics></math>.

A problem that asks how fast one quantity changes, given how fast related quantities change: write an equation linking them, differentiate with respect to time, then substitute the values at the instant in question.

A relative (local) maximum is a value <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(c)</annotation></semantics></math> with <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≥</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(c) \ge f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> for every <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> in some open interval around <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>; a relative minimum has <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≤</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(c) \le f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> there. It is a peak or valley compared with nearby points only.
terms.topicTitle: Extreme Value Theorem, Global and Local Extrema, Critical Points

terms.def: A discontinuity at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = c</annotation></semantics></math> where <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></munder><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{x \to c} f(x)</annotation></semantics></math> exists, but <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(c)</annotation></semantics></math> is undefined or not equal to it. The graph has a hole, possibly with a dot elsewhere above or below it.

Making a function continuous at a point by choosing its value there, or a constant in its formula. A removable discontinuity is removed by defining <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(c)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></munder><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \lim_{x \to c} f(x)</annotation></semantics></math>; a piecewise function is made continuous at a break point by choosing constants so both pieces and the value agree. Jump and infinite discontinuities cannot be removed this way.

Revolving a region about a line other than an axis, such as <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = k</annotation></semantics></math> or <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = h</annotation></semantics></math>. The radius is the distance from that line to the curve: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r = |f(x) - k|</annotation></semantics></math> for a horizontal line, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r = |h - x(y)|</annotation></semantics></math> for a vertical one.

An estimate of the accumulated change (the area under a graph) built from rectangles: split the interval into subintervals and add up (width) times (a height of the function on that subinterval). A left sum uses each subinterval's left end, a right sum its right end, a midpoint sum its middle.
A line through two points of a graph. Its slope is the average rate of change of the function between those two inputs.
terms.topicTitle: Average and Instantaneous Rates of Change

terms.def: The derivative of the derivative: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">″</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f''(x) = \frac{d}{dx}f'(x)</annotation></semantics></math>, also written <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}</annotation></semantics></math>. It measures how fast <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'</annotation></semantics></math> changes. Higher-order derivatives continue: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">‴</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'''</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{(4)}</annotation></semantics></math>, ..., <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{(n)}</annotation></semantics></math>.

If <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'(c) = 0</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">″</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f''(c) > 0</annotation></semantics></math>, then <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> has a relative minimum at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>; if <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'(c) = 0</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">″</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo><</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f''(c) < 0</annotation></semantics></math>, a relative maximum. If <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">″</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f''(c) = 0</annotation></semantics></math>, the test gives no conclusion.

A way to solve <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{dy}{dx} = g(x)h(y)</annotation></semantics></math>: move every <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> to the side with <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">dy</annotation></semantics></math> and every <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> to the side with <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">dx</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{h(y)}\,dy = g(x)\,dx</annotation></semantics></math>, then integrate both sides and add one constant <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math>. The result, a family with <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> in it, is the general solution.
terms.topicTitle: General Solutions by Separation of Variables

terms.def: Shorthand for a sum: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i</annotation></semantics></math> means <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mo>⋯</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n</annotation></semantics></math>. A Riemann sum with right ends is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munderover><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i)\,\Delta x</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta x = \frac{b - a}{n}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_i = a + i\,\Delta x</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Riemann Sums, Sigma Notation and the Definite Integral

terms.def: The value of a definite integral read from a graph: areas of regions above the x-axis count as positive and areas below count as negative, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int_a^b f(x)\,dx</annotation></semantics></math> = (area above) minus (area below).

Triangles with the same three angles. Their corresponding sides are in the same ratio, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>h</mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>R</mi><mi>H</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{r}{h} = \frac{R}{H}</annotation></semantics></math> for matching sides.

Sine and cosine give the coordinates of the point at angle <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> on the unit circle: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>. The others are ratios: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>tan</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tan\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>sec</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sec\theta = \frac{1}{\cos\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>csc</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\csc\theta = \frac{1}{\sin\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>cot</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cot\theta = \frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>.

Rise over run: for a line through <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x_1, y_1)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x_2, y_2)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}</annotation></semantics></math>.

A picture of a differential equation <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{dy}{dx} = F(x, y)</annotation></semantics></math>: at each chosen point <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x, y)</annotation></semantics></math>, a short segment with slope <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F(x, y)</annotation></semantics></math>. A solution curve through a point follows the segments near it.

A function that makes a differential equation true for every <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> in an interval: substitute it and its derivatives, and the two sides are equal. To verify a solution, differentiate, substitute and compare.

The absolute value of velocity, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|v(t)|</annotation></semantics></math>: how fast an object moves, whatever its direction. Speed is never negative.

A particle is speeding up when its speed <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|v|</annotation></semantics></math> increases, which happens when <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v(t)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a(t)</annotation></semantics></math> have the same sign; it is slowing down when they have opposite signs.

Breaking an area integral at every point where the curves cross, so each piece uses top minus bottom (or right minus left) and every piece adds a positive area. Equivalent to integrating <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|f(x) - g(x)|</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Area Between Curves That Cross More Than Twice

terms.def: If <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≤</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≤</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g(x) \le f(x) \le h(x)</annotation></semantics></math> for every <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> near <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> (except possibly at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>), and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></munder><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{x \to c} g(x)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></munder><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \lim_{x \to c} h(x)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= L</annotation></semantics></math>, then <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></munder><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L</annotation></semantics></math>. Also called the sandwich theorem.

One of the pieces an interval is split into for a Riemann or trapezoidal sum. Subintervals may have equal widths (from a formula) or unequal widths (from the times in a table); each width is the difference of its two ends.

The line through <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a, f(a))</annotation></semantics></math> whose slope is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'(a)</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)</annotation></semantics></math>. It is the limit of secant lines through that point.

The length of the path a particle travels over a time interval, counting motion in both directions as positive: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int_a^b |v(t)|\,dt</annotation></semantics></math>, the integral of speed.

An estimate of the area under a graph built from trapezoids: on each subinterval, the width times the average of the function's values at the two ends. It equals the average of the left and right Riemann sums that use the same subintervals.

A slice of a solid shaped like a triangle or a semicircle, standing on a segment of length <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> across the base. Areas: equilateral triangle <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt><mn>4</mn></mfrac><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}s^2</annotation></semantics></math>; isosceles right triangle with a leg in the base <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{2}s^2</annotation></semantics></math>, with the hypotenuse in the base <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{4}s^2</annotation></semantics></math>; semicircle with diameter <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>8</mn></mfrac><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\pi}{8}s^2</annotation></semantics></math>.
terms.topicTitle: Volumes with Triangle and Semicircle Cross Sections

terms.def: Undoing the chain rule: when an integrand has the form <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(g(x))\,g'(x)</annotation></semantics></math>, let <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u = g(x)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">du = g'(x)\,dx</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int f(g(x))g'(x)\,dx</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \int f(u)\,du</annotation></semantics></math>. In a definite integral the limits change to <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u = g(a)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u = g(b)</annotation></semantics></math>.
Outputs that grow larger and larger in size without any bound, as near a vertical asymptote. Oscillating behavior is outputs that keep swinging between values and never settle.

The circle of radius 1 centered at the origin, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^2 + y^2 = 1</annotation></semantics></math>. The point at angle <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> (measured counterclockwise from <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(1, 0)</annotation></semantics></math>) is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>.

The rate of change of position: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v(t) = x'(t)</annotation></semantics></math>. Its sign gives the direction of motion and its absolute value the speed. Units: distance per time.

Volume of a cone <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>h</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h</annotation></semantics></math>, of a cylinder <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>h</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi r^2 h</annotation></semantics></math>, of a sphere <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>4</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3</annotation></semantics></math>; area of a trapezoid <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>h</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{b_1 + b_2}{2}h</annotation></semantics></math>, of a semicircle <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{2}\pi r^2</annotation></semantics></math>.

The washer method with the axis of rotation on a line <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = k</annotation></semantics></math> or <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = h</annotation></semantics></math>. Both radii are distances from that line: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> to the edge of the region farther from the line, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> to the nearer edge, and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V = \pi\int \left(R^2 - r^2\right)</annotation></semantics></math>.

The volume of a solid of revolution whose slices have a hole: each slice is a washer with outer radius <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> (axis to the far edge of the region) and inner radius <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> (axis to the near edge), so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>π</mi><msubsup><mo largeop="true" movablelimits="false">∫</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \pi\int_a^b \left(R^2 - r^2\right)\,dx</annotation></semantics></math>.
